case_study_insert.main_stem: Valbruna Ski Chalets (VSC) is a private limited company in the alpine hospitality sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2012 by Elena Marchetti, the business operates six timber chalets offering guided ski holidays, with a flat organisational structure and democratic leadership. VSC plans to invest $720,000 in six new eco-chalets with snowmaking equipment, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $222,000 a year, a variable cost of $48 a unit and a selling price of $85, and currently produces 12,000 units a year. VSC faces two operational problems: seasonal absenteeism has reached 8% and customer complaints about slow room turnaround are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Winter 2025: The six chalets hosted 5,400 guest-nights last quarter at an average occupancy of 81%. Customer complaints about turnaround fell from 24 to 12 per month and the defect rate on chalet repairs dropped to 1.5%. Market research of 520 guests found that 63% would pay up to $15 more per night for certified eco-timber chalets, and 49% check a resort's sustainability rating before booking. A skills audit shows 17 of 40 employees have not completed on-the-job training on the new check-in tablets; off-the-job training courses at the regional college cost $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Valbruna Ski Chalets as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, the third rise this year, increasing costs for variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $11.80 to $12.53 per hour from April 2026, raising seasonal wage bills. (3) Heating fuel and timber input costs have risen 11.8% year-on-year, and leisure inflation is running at 7.6%, while consumer spending on winter sports holidays grew 4.9% in the same period.

questions.question_text: VSC plans to finance its eco-chalet expansion partly with retained profit. Explain two advantages for VSC of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the $450,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charges or repayment schedule, which protects VSC's cash flow at a time when it already faces fixed costs of $222,000 a year and a $450,000 ten-year loan commitment. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 11.8% rise in heating fuel and timber input costs, helping VSC defend its $85 selling price and its margin on 12,000 units a year while the six eco-chalets bed in.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repossession risk attached to the bank loan, so the $270,000 from retained profit is available without putting the new $720,000 eco-chalet site at risk if snowfall or bookings disappoint. It also preserves Elena Marchetti's ownership and control — no external lender can impose conditions on how the snowmaking equipment or eco-chalets are operated, and VSC's flat structure with democratic leadership keeps decision-making with the founder and staff.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Valbruna Ski Chalets and its eco-chalet expansion decision.

questions.question_text: VSC is launching its six new eco-chalets. Consider a national ski-magazine print campaign, a partnership with ski travel influencers on social media, or sponsorship of the regional winter sports television broadcast. Which should VSC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National ski-magazine print campaign: A dedicated feature across leading ski magazines would reach affluent winter-sports readers who trust specialist print advice and would match VSC's premium eco-timber positioning. However, print readership is declining, lead times are long, and much of the national readership would be outside chalet catchment or already booked, so cost per confirmed booking could be high for a 40-employee business funding a $720,000 expansion.

Ski travel influencer marketing: Partnering with respected ski and mountain-lifestyle influencers would target exactly the 63% of 520 surveyed guests willing to pay up to $15 more per night for certified eco-chalets and the 49% who check sustainability ratings before booking. Content can be tracked through booking codes, and influencers scale nationally at modest cost, though results build more slowly than broadcast and depend on influencer credibility.

Regional winter sports television sponsorship: TV sponsorship would deliver broad mass awareness quickly across the winter season and associate VSC with the sport it serves. Its weakness is wastage — many viewers never take alpine holidays, airtime costs are high, and coverage is regional rather than national, limiting the value for a business receiving guests from across the country.

Recommendation: VSC should choose ski travel influencer marketing. It reaches the precise eco-conscious segment already identified in its research, costs far less than television print production and airtime, scales nationally like regional TV cannot, and turns the $15 per-night eco premium into visible, shareable proof. The ski-magazine campaign is rejected as too slow and poorly targeted for a measured launch; regional television sponsorship is rejected as too expensive and too broad for a 40-person operator funding a bank-loan-financed expansion; a small in-store regional college partnership and guest referral scheme can supplement influencers later.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to VSC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VSC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of VSC with a well-justified recommendation explaining why the print campaign and television sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: VSC's seasonal absenteeism has reached 8%. Explain two benefits for VSC of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its chalet and housekeeping team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives VSC's 40 employees a genuine voice in rotas, turnaround routines and snowmaking priorities, which satisfies their social and esteem needs and raises job satisfaction. Staff who help design the turnaround checklist that drove complaints down from 24 to 12 per month are more likely to attend reliably, directly attacking the 8% seasonal absenteeism rate and relieving pressure on a flat organisational structure.

Point 2: Involving housekeeping and chalet staff generates practical suggestions from the people who fix rooms daily, improving guest experience and reducing the 1.5% repair defect rate further. Higher involvement raises commitment and lowers labour turnover, saving the $750 per employee off-the-job course cost for the 17 of 40 staff not yet trained on the check-in tablets, and protecting output of 12,000 units a year while the six eco-chalets come online.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VSC's absenteeism, quality and output.

questions.question_text: VSC must upskill 17 staff to operate the new check-in tablets and guest eco-chalets. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional college. Which should VSC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training on the chalet floor is directly relevant to VSC's own check-in tablets, room-turnaround sequence and snowkeeping protocols, costs nothing in fees, and keeps the 17 staff productive through the 81% occupancy season. Its weaknesses are that trainer colleagues lose productive time, bad habits can be copied, and there is no formal certificate, which matters if auditors or tour operators demand documented training records for eco-certification.

Off-the-job training: The regional college course at $750 per employee gives structured, certified training for all 17 staff, costing $12,750 in total — affordable within a $720,000 expansion budget. Certification supports the eco-timber accreditation guests read on sustainability ratings. Its drawbacks are the $12,750 fee, staff time away from the chalets during peak weeks, and content that is generic rather than specific to VSC's tablets and turnaround sequence.

Decision: VSC should choose on-the-job training for the immediate rollout, with a short off-the-job top-up at the college for two senior chalet leads. On-the-job training is cheapest, machine-and-eco-chalet-specific and avoids further output loss while absenteeism is already 8%; full off-the-job training is rejected because withholding $12,750 and losing 17 staff during an 81%-occupancy season would hurt guest turnaround and the 12,000-unit target, and certification can be added later once tablet routines stabilise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to VSC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of VSC.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of VSC with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and certificate relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VSC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $222,000 ÷ ($85 − $48) = $222,000 ÷ $37 = 6,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 6,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $85 − $48 = $37.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $37.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VSC's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 6,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 12,000 units to confirm the chalet operation is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 6,000 units, informing whether to accelerate eco-chalet bookings in shoulder seasons.
2. Contribution per unit of $37.00 lets VSC model the effect of the $15 per-night eco premium, for example a discounted winter package at $75 would cut contribution to $27.00, letting managers judge whether extra guest-nights would still cover the $222,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $222,000 and contribution per unit helps managers set the volume targets used to justify the $450,000 bank loan repayments and to check the new eco-chalets service them before committing the further $270,000 retained profit.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($222,000 ÷ 12,000 units + $48 = $66.50 a unit) to benchmark seasonal performance, identify waste behind rising turnaround complaints, and decide whether to renegotiate the $48 variable cost with linen and heating suppliers amid the 11.8% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 6,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $37.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 12,000-unit output; eco-premium and discount modelling vs $222,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $720,000 eco-chalet expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $66.50 to tackle waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VSC's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has VSC's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.44 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.56 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.04 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $55,000 trade receivables + $35,000 cash = $180,000; 2025 = $65,000 + $75,000 + $55,000 = $195,000. Liquidity 2024 = $180,000 ÷ $125,000 = 1.44; 2025 = $195,000 ÷ $125,000 = 1.56. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($180,000 − $90,000) ÷ $125,000 = $90,000 ÷ $125,000 = 0.72; 2025 = ($195,000 − $65,000) ÷ $125,000 = $130,000 ÷ $125,000 = 1.04.

Evaluation: Liquidity has clearly strengthened. The 2025 liquidity figure improved from 1.44 to 1.56, meaning current assets cover current liabilities more comfortably, helped by cash rising from $35,000 to $55,000 and inventories falling from $90,000 to $65,000. The stricter liquidity measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.72 to 1.04, so VSC no longer relies on selling stock to meet short-term debts — critical while it services a $450,000 bank loan and funds a $720,000 eco-chalet expansion. However, trade receivables rose from $55,000 to $75,000, tying up cash; if tour operators pay late, the stronger ratios could deteriorate quickly, and inventories fell sharply, so chalet stock availability for peak weeks should be monitored.

Conclusion: VSC's financial position has improved. Both the 2024-to-2025 liquidity measures (1.44 to 1.56, and 0.72 to 1.04) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not depend on inventory. The main residual risk is rising trade receivables, so VSC should tighten deposit and credit terms with travel partners while proceeding with the eco-chalet expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether VSC's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VSC of introducing eco-timber construction and snowmaking for its new eco-chalets.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Eco-timber chalets match the preferences of the 63% of 520 surveyed guests willing to pay up to $15 more per night, allowing VSC to charge a premium that protects its $37.00 contribution per unit even as heating fuel and timber input costs rise 11.8%. They also strengthen VSC's position with the 49% of guests who check sustainability ratings before booking, helping secure tour-operator listings and justify the $720,000 expansion.

Disadvantage: Sustainable timber and snowmaking equipment typically cost more than conventional build and imported energy, which would increase the $48 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the $15 premium is accepted across the booking calendar. Any failure in eco-materials or snowmaking reliability (for example higher repair frequency or downtime) would also raise the current 1.5% repair defect rate and erode the 81% occupancy that the expansion depends on.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to VSC's research data, costs and eco-chalet expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase to $12.53 per hour, and the 11.8% rise in heating fuel and timber input costs will affect VSC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If VSC's $450,000 ten-year bank loan carries a variable rate, annual interest rises by roughly 0.75%, adding about $3,375 a year to financing costs and slightly raising the burden above the $222,000 fixed costs. Higher rates may also cool consumer appetite for premium ski holidays, which could soften the 4.9% growth in winter-sports spending. The direct impact is real but modest, and VSC can partly shield itself by negotiating a fixed rate on the loan.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $12.53 per hour): With 40 employees, mainly seasonal chalet, housekeeping and front-desk roles, the lowest-paid roughly 20 workers would each see about 6.2% added to their hourly pay; at around $12.53 per hour and seasonal hours, the combined effect is roughly $20,000 a year, which democratic leadership, productivity gains (12,000 units ÷ 40 staff = 300 guest-nights per worker) and the $15 eco premium would need to offset.

Input cost inflation (11.8% heating fuel and timber): VSC's $48 variable cost is dominated by heating and timber-related supplies, roughly $26 per guest-night. An 11.8% rise on that portion adds about $3.07 per unit; at 12,000 units that is roughly $36,800 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $37.00 toward $34.00 and reducing profit, though VSC can partially recover through the $15 eco premium and renegotiated supplier contracts.

Conclusion: The 11.8% rise in heating fuel and timber input costs will have the greatest impact. It repeatedly erodes the $37.00 contribution on every one of the 12,000 units sold, totalling roughly $36,800 a year and threatening the margin that justifies the $720,000 eco-chalet expansion. The minimum wage increase is the second most serious risk at roughly $20,000 a year, while the interest-rate rise is the smallest in cash terms at about $3,375 and can be managed by fixing the loan rate; all three still require VSC to prioritise cost control and premium pricing.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to VSC.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on VSC's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of VSC with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
